issues.legal_issue: A court may add a party despite the plaintiff’s choice of defendants only when that person is necessary or proper for effective and complete adjudication of the questions in the suit.
material_facts: The plaintiff objected to adding the lessee as a defendant, arguing that he was dominus litis and claimed no relief against it.
The lessee sought to be joined, asserting that it had evidence about the alleged unauthorised constructions and an interest in the premises.
issues.conclusion: A plaintiff’s status as dominus litis does not prevent the court from adding a defendant, but the court may add only a necessary or proper party whose presence meets the requirements for effective and complete adjudication.
issues.legal_principle: Order I, Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 gives the court discretion to add parties at any stage. A necessary party is one without whom no effective order can be made; a proper party is one whose presence is needed for a complete and final decision on the questions involved. A person’s relevant evidence or interest in the correct resolution of a question alone is insufficient: the person must have a direct or legal interest such that the result may affect their legal rights. The Court relied on Razia Begum v. Anwar Begum, [1959] SCR 1111, and referred to Amon v. Raphael Tuck & Sons Ltd., (1956) 1 All E.R. 273, and Dollfus Mieg et Compagnie S.A. v. Bank of England, (1950) 2 All E.R. 611.

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit in which the court is considering whether to add a person as a party.
predicates.party_needed_for_effective_order_or_comp: The person’s presence is necessary to make an effective order or to reach a complete and final decision on the questions in the suit.

issues.definition: When a person’s presence is needed for an effective order or complete adjudication in a civil suit, the court may add that person despite the plaintiff’s objection.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee is not a necessary or proper party to a suit challenging a demolition notice directed at the plaintiff when the lessee has no direct legal interest in the structures targeted and its potential claim against the plaintiff arises from a separate cause of action.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued the municipal authority to challenge a notice requiring demolition of two structures that the plaintiff allegedly erected without authorisation.
The lessee held the land and service-station premises but had no interest in the two structures targeted by the notice.
The lessee claimed to have evidence that the structures were unauthorised, but no notice had been issued to it and no collusion between the plaintiff and the municipal authority was alleged.
Any grievance the lessee might have against the plaintiff for breach of their agreement would arise from a different cause of action.
issues.conclusion: The lessee was neither a necessary nor a proper party to the suit, and the courts below erred in ordering its addition as a defendant.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order I, Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, a person must have a direct or legal interest in the subject matter, and the person’s presence must be necessary for effective and complete adjudication. Relevant evidence, a commercial interest, a desire to advance arguments, or the possibility of avoiding another suit does not alone justify joinder. The Court relied on Razia Begum v. Anwar Begum, [1959] SCR 1111; distinguished National Textile Workers’ Union v. P.R. Ramakrishnan, [1983] 1 SCR 922; and referred to Amon v. Raphael Tuck & Sons Ltd., (1956) 1 All E.R. 273, and Dollfus Mieg et Compagnie S.A. v. Bank of England, (1950) 2 All E.R. 611.

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_public_demolition: The plaintiff brings a civil suit challenging a public authority’s notice requiring demolition.
predicates.notice_targets_structures_erected_by_pla: The demolition notice concerns structures allegedly erected by the plaintiff, rather than structures in which the intervener has a direct legal interest.
predicates.intervener_has_no_direct_legal_interest_: The proposed intervener’s legal rights are not affected by the outcome concerning the targeted structures.
predicates.intervener_offers_only_evidence: The proposed intervener seeks to participate because it can provide evidence relevant to whether the structures are unauthorised.
predicates.intervener_has_only_separate_contract_cl: Any claim the proposed intervener may have against the plaintiff arises from a contractual dispute distinct from the demolition-notice challenge.

issues.definition: If a demolition-notice suit concerns the plaintiff’s structures, the proposed intervener lacks a direct legal interest in them, and the intervener offers only evidence or has only a separate contractual claim, the intervener is not a necessary or proper party.
